idiom_name: goroutines over the runtime-integrated network poller
implementation_notes: The Go runtime implements the pattern for the programmer: a goroutine that performs network I/O is parked by the scheduler, and the integrated network poller (epoll, kqueue, I/O completion ports - see runtime/netpoll.go) unparks it when the descriptor is ready, so Read and Write look blocking while the runtime performs the completion dispatch. The processor and dispatcher roles are internal and the handler is the continuation of the goroutine; explicit callbacks are needed only where a library exposes them. Per-goroutine buffers replace the explicit ownership discipline that manual implementations require.
pitfalls: The poller covers network I/O and timers; ordinary file I/O and cgo calls occupy an operating-system thread instead, so heavy blocking work needs its own accounting or pool.
Goroutine-per-connection has no bound: without limits on accepted work, memory grows with connections rather than with capacity.
Timeouts and cancellation are per-connection (SetDeadline) and propagate only where the code checks contexts; a missing deadline leaves goroutines parked indefinitely.
